problem_summary.summary: Return the number of set bits in the binary representation of a positive integer.
problem_summary.input_output: Input: positive integer n. Output: its Hamming weight, the count of bits equal to 1.

brute_force.explanation: Inspect each of the 32 positions with a mask and increment the count whenever that position is set. This predictable scan is useful as a simple reference implementation.
brute_force.correctness_idea: Every bit position is checked exactly once, and each set position contributes one to the count.
brute_force.time_complexity: O(32) = O(1) for a fixed-width integer.

optimized.explanation: Use Brian Kernighan's operation n & (n - 1), which clears the rightmost set bit. Repeat until n becomes zero; the number of iterations equals the number of set bits.
optimized.correctness_idea: Each update removes exactly one set bit and never changes any other set bit. The loop stops only after every original set bit has been removed, so its iteration count is the Hamming weight.
optimized.time_complexity: O(k), where k is the number of set bits; worst case O(32) = O(1) for a fixed-width integer.

steps.event: Clear the next rightmost set bit.
Clear the next rightmost set bit.

steps.action: Compute 32 & 31 = 0; increment count, then the loop ends.

edge_cases.case: n is a power of two
edge_cases.handling: Exactly one set bit is cleared, so the result is 1.

edge_cases.case: n has all 31 allowed bits set
edge_cases.handling: The optimized loop runs once per set bit; the scan checks all positions and both return 31.
Although excluded by the stated constraint, both implementations naturally return 0.
